clue.text: Was this early work a breeze for Gore Vidal?

definitions.text: Was this early work a breeze for Gore Vidal?

parts.words: Was this early work a breeze for Gore Vidal?
parts.note: asks for the title of Gore Vidal's first novel, written at nineteen, which is also the name of a sudden violent gust of wind off mountains

explanation.surface: Did Gore Vidal find writing his first book easy?
explanation.walkthrough: 'A breeze' reads as 'an easy job', but it is literal: the title of Vidal's 1946 debut novel is a word for a fierce squall, so the book really was a wind.
explanation.definitionFit: Vidal's debut novel of 1946, set on an army ship in the Aleutians, takes its title from the local name for a sudden mountain squall.

parts.note: a composer whose surname is the name of an island nation, so he is 'insular' in the literal sense

explanation.definitionFit: John Ireland was an English composer of songs and piano music, and his surname names an island, hence 'insular'.

definitions.meaning: Robert Dudley, Elizabeth I's favourite, was made Earl of this place and appears as such in Scott's novel Kenilworth
a city in the English Midlands run by a single tier of local government

explanation.walkthrough: 'of Kenilworth' belongs to the first definition: Dudley is the Earl in Scott's Kenilworth. Dudley is also a West Midlands town, a false trail towards place-names.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Dudley was created Earl of the Midland city of that name, and that city is a single-tier local council area.

clue.text: Seafood favoured by Arabella Allen Dickens's monocular dominie

definitions.meaning: a small edible sea snail eaten picked out with a pin
in Dickens's Pickwick Papers Arabella Allen elopes with and marries Nathaniel, one of the Pickwickians

explanation.walkthrough: The words 'Dickens's monocular dominie' are 5-down's clue, run into this one by the printed text; they play no part here.
explanation.definitionFit: A small edible sea snail shares its name with the Pickwickian whom Arabella Allen chose to marry.

parts.note: the one-eyed, brutal schoolmaster of Dotheboys Hall in Nicholas Nickleby

explanation.walkthrough: A dominie is a Scottish word for a schoolmaster; monocular means one-eyed.
explanation.definitionFit: The one-eyed headmaster of Dotheboys Hall in Nicholas Nickleby is Dickens's best-known cruel teacher.

indicators.note: letters at odds with one another are set in a new order, so the word themes is rearranged

explanation.surface: A critic finds clashing motifs in a J. B. Priestley character.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conflicting' rearranges THEMES. The answer is the downtrodden cashier in Priestley's novel Angel Pavement.
explanation.definitionFit: Mr Smeeth is the anxious clerk of the London firm in J. B. Priestley's 1930 novel Angel Pavement.

parts.note: points to the American novelist who published a novel titled with an exclamation, Oil!, in that year

explanation.definitionFit: Upton Sinclair's 1927 novel Oil! fictionalised the California petroleum boom, so the writer 'struck oil' in print.

clue.text: Miss St Clare takes wrong line in work admired by Jane Austen

indicators.note: one piece takes in the other, holding it inside itself

parts.note: Eva St Clare is the saintly child in Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin

indicators.note: set wrong, the letters of line are put in another order

explanation.surface: A young girl from a famous novel misreads a line in a book Jane Austen loved.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrong' turns LINE into ELIN, and EVA 'takes' it inside: EV-ELIN-A. Fanny Burney's novel was a favourite of Austen's.
explanation.definitionFit: Fanny Burney's epistolary novel of 1778 was much praised by Austen, who defended novels by naming it in Northanger Abbey.

clue.text: "the most I can do for him, is to consider him a respectable " (Lord Chesterfield)

definitions.text: "the most I can do for him, is to consider him a respectable " (Lord Chesterfield)

parts.words: "the most I can do for him, is to consider him a respectable " (Lord Chesterfield)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap: Chesterfield's letter describing an uncouth acquaintance, generally taken to be Dr Johnson, with a dated term for a southern African people

explanation.walkthrough: The solver fills the gap in Chesterfield's letter to his son (1751). The word is now regarded as offensive for the Khoekhoe people.
explanation.definitionFit: Chesterfield's letter calls an ill-mannered man of learning a respectable savage, using the old European name for the Khoekhoe of southern Africa.

clue.text: Greek stones to be heaped on Latin bones

definitions.text: Greek stones to be heaped on Latin bones

parts.words: Greek stones to be heaped on Latin bones
parts.note: recalls the myth of the giants piling one Greek mountain on another, Mount Ossa, whose name in Latin means bones

explanation.walkthrough: 'Piling Pelion on Ossa' comes from the giants' attempt to reach heaven; 'ossa' is also Latin for bones, so the mountain of stones goes on top of the bones.
explanation.definitionFit: Pelion is the Thessalian mountain the giants heaped on Mount Ossa, whose name matches the Latin plural for bones.

definitions.meaning: a win, especially taking territory by force
Robert, a poet and historian who edited New Lines, the anthology of the 1950s Movement group

explanation.definitionFit: A triumph that subdues an enemy, and the surname of Robert, editor of the 1956 Movement anthology New Lines.

clue.text: Swedish Nobel prizewinner applies for legal changes

indicators.note: the words for legal undergo changes, their letters being shuffled into a new order

explanation.surface: A Swedish laureate files to have the law altered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'changes' rearranges FOR LEGAL. Selma Lagerlöf, author of The Wonderful Adventures of Nils, was the first woman to win the Nobel Prize for Literature (1909).
explanation.definitionFit: Selma Lagerlöf, the Swedish novelist, won the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1909, the first woman to do so.

parts.note: names the novel Madame de... and asks for the first name of the French woman who wrote it, filling the gap before 'de Vilmorin'

explanation.definitionFit: The 1951 novella Madame de... was written by the French poet and novelist Louise de Vilmorin, later filmed by Max Ophüls.

clue.text: Dramatist makes first try in long poems

indicators.note: one piece is placed in the other, inside it

parts.note: odes are lyric poems, often long and formal

indicators.note: first picks the opening letter of the word try

explanation.surface: A playwright debuts by attempting extended verse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'first' takes T from 'try', and 'in' sets it inside ODES. Clifford Odets wrote Waiting for Lefty and Golden Boy.
explanation.definitionFit: Clifford Odets was the American playwright of the 1930s Group Theatre, author of Waiting for Lefty.

clue.text: Old boy meeting magnificent in Douglas

parts.note: OB is the abbreviation for old boy, a former pupil of a school
a session is a meeting or sitting of a body

explanation.surface: A former pupil turns up at a grand reunion in the Isle of Man's capital.
explanation.walkthrough: Douglas looks like the Manx town, but it is Lloyd C. Douglas, whose novel is Magnificent Obsession: the answer is the word that follows 'magnificent' in that title.
explanation.definitionFit: Lloyd C. Douglas's 1929 bestseller is Magnificent Obsession, so the word completing his title is a fixation.

clue.text: French kings get translated arts from poet-chronicler

parts.note: with French in play, kings are taken in that language, rois

indicators.note: translated here means turned into another form, so the letters of arts are rearranged

explanation.surface: A medieval chronicler of French royalty has his works rendered into English.
explanation.walkthrough: 'translated' rearranges ARTS as SART. Jean Froissart wrote the chronicles of the Hundred Years' War and was also a court poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Jean Froissart, the fourteenth-century French writer, wrote both the Chronicles of the Hundred Years' War and courtly verse.

clue.text: Article she enclosed to doctor in council at Jerusalem

indicators.note: with the article enclosed, the word she is wrapped round it

parts.note: an is the indefinite article
taken as written

explanation.surface: A woman sends a piece to a physician working in the governing body of Jerusalem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'enclosed' puts AN inside SHE, giving S-AN-HE; DR and IN follow. 'Doctor' looks like a verb but is the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sanhedrin was the supreme Jewish court and assembly sitting in Jerusalem in the time of the Second Temple.

indicators.note: a sort of create in is a loose version of those words, their letters in another order

explanation.surface: A composer is told to build something out of a kind of refrain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sort of' rearranges CREATE IN. The answer is a rare word for repeating something.
explanation.definitionFit: Iterance is a literary word for the act of repeating, from the same root as iterate.

parts.note: spirit is distilled alcoholic drink
SO is the abbreviation for standing order, a regular bank payment instruction

explanation.surface: A drink with an antique rule of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the musical direction for a lively, spirited performance. A standing order is a British term for an instruction to a bank to make a regular payment.
explanation.definitionFit: In music, spiritoso marks a passage to be played with spirit and animation.

clue.text: Some artists lay it on a bit thick!

definitions.text: Some artists lay it on a bit thick!

parts.words: Some artists lay it on a bit thick!
parts.note: reads as an accusation of exaggeration, but describes painters applying paint thickly so brush or knife marks stand out

explanation.definitionFit: Impasto is the technique of laying paint on a canvas so heavily that it stands in relief.

indicators.note: the content of the string is what lies inside it, so the answer is found within these letters

parts.note: the answer to 7-down, the Burney novel, followed by the letters pt and ii as printed

explanation.surface: An unfitting passage appears in the second part of a novel.
explanation.walkthrough: Write out 7-down's answer followed by PT II; 'content of' picks the letters inside: evel-INA PT-ii. The bracket looks like a reference to Part Two.
explanation.definitionFit: Inapt means not suited to the purpose or occasion.

parts.note: past means former, of an earlier time
EUR is an abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A famous scientist was once a European.
explanation.walkthrough: Louis Pasteur, French chemist and microbiologist, devised pasteurisation and the rabies vaccine.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Pasteur is the French scientist famous for pasteurisation and vaccines.

indicators.note: spoken signals a word as it sounds when said, not as it is written

parts.note: whimsy is caprice, a playful fancy

explanation.surface: Detective fiction's fanciful streak, as voiced by its author.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spoken' gives the sound of WHIMSY. Lord Peter Wimsey is the aristocratic detective of Dorothy L. Sayers's novels.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Peter is the gentleman sleuth created by the novelist Dorothy L. Sayers.

clue.text: Composer with right to late meal

parts.note: Franz von Suppé was the Austrian composer of the Light Cavalry overture

explanation.surface: A musician who stays up and then eats in the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: Suppé, composer of the Poet and Peasant overture, plus R.
explanation.definitionFit: Supper is the last meal of the day, taken in the evening.

parts.note: uni is short for university, a college
verse is lines of poetry

explanation.surface: A university's verses by a contemporary British poet.
explanation.walkthrough: Christopher Reid's 1996 collection is Expanded Universes, so his book stands for the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The British poet Christopher Reid titled a collection Expanded Universes, so the cosmos word comes from his book.

clue.text: Example this month — article on the church

parts.note: inst., short for instant, means of this month in old business letters
an is the indefinite article
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: An example of a note dated this month about a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Inst.' was used in commercial letters: 'yours of the 5th inst.' means the fifth of this month.
explanation.definitionFit: An instance is a single case or example of something.

parts.note: points to Elmer Rice's Pulitzer play whose title is a scene of urban life, the word before 'Scene' in that title

explanation.definitionFit: Elmer Rice's 1929 Pulitzer-winning play Street Scene is set outside a New York tenement.

clue.text: "… trip, like the s of Hog's-Norton, where the pigs play on the organ" (Scott, Woodstock)

definitions.text: "… trip, like the s of Hog's-Norton, where the pigs play on the organ" (Scott, Woodstock)

parts.words: "… trip, like the s of Hog's-Norton, where the pigs play on the organ" (Scott, Woodstock)
parts.note: a quotation with a gap before the printed 's': the word wanted means a simpleton, here plural, the fools of a proverbial Oxfordshire village

explanation.walkthrough: Fill the gap in Scott's line; the trailing 's' makes it plural. Hog's Norton (Hook Norton, Oxfordshire) was proverbial for rustic fools.
explanation.definitionFit: A noodle is an old word for a simpleton, and Scott's line mocks the fools of Hog's Norton.

parts.note: James Michener's 1954 novel of the Korean War era takes its title from the Japanese word of farewell

explanation.definitionFit: James Michener's novel set in Japan bears the Japanese word for goodbye as its title, so the book is a farewell.
